slides.name: 4 · Check · From last week · 1

params.text: Notes closed. Temperature in °C: what kind of attribute is it?
Nominal: the numbers are just labels
Ordinal: ordered, but the gaps mean nothing
Interval: equal gaps, but no true zero
Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero

slides.notes:
2 min. Retrieval from Week 2, notes closed. Take answers, ask for the reason, then reveal. If most pick ratio, spend a minute on what a true zero means: it decides whether “twice as much” is a sentence you may say.

20°C is 10 degrees warmer than 10°C, so differences mean something. But 0°C is not “no temperature”, so 20°C is not twice as hot. Equal gaps without a true zero is interval.

slides.name: 9 · Section · Four levels, three questions

params.text: Munzner’s nested model: What? Why? How?

slides.notes: ≈20 min for this section. The framework is the vocabulary for everything after it.

slides.name: 10 · Four levels, three questions

params.text: You are asked to build a dashboard. Where do you start: with the users, the data, the chart or the code?

params.data:
Level	Asks	Threat
Domain situation	Who are the target users?|What do they need to do?	You misunderstood|their needs
Data/task abstraction	What is shown? (data)|Why are they looking? (task)	You’re showing them|the wrong thing
Idiom	How is it shown? (encoding)|How is it manipulated? (interaction)	The way you show it|doesn’t work
Algorithm	How is it computed|efficiently?	Your code is|too slow
params.source: After Munzner (2009), A Nested Model for Visualization Design and Validation.
params.prompt: You are asked to build a dashboard. Where do you start: with the users, the data, the chart or the code?

slides.notes:
Take a few answers to the prompt first. Then step through: each level lights while the others dim. Domain: who are the users and what do they need. Abstraction: What? (data) and Why? (task), in the vocabulary of vis. Idiom: How? (encoding and interaction). Algorithm: efficient computation. Four threats: each level has its own way to fail; an outer failure cascades inward, so a perfect algorithm cannot save the wrong idiom. Work top-down from a problem (problem-driven) or bottom-up from a technique.
Source: Munzner (2009); adapted from the supplied Week 3 lecture materials (title typo “Farmwork” fixed). The original figure is redrawn natively.
Step captions in full: Domain: The outer box: the people and their problem. Everything else sits inside it, so nothing inside can rescue a misunderstood domain. Abstraction: Translate the domain into vis vocabulary: what is shown (data abstraction) and why the user is looking (task abstraction). What? and Why? live here. Idiom: How? The visual encoding (how to draw it) and the interaction (how to manipulate it). Algorithm: The innermost box: compute it efficiently. A fast algorithm cannot save the wrong idiom. Four threats: Each level has its own way to fail. A failure at an outer level cascades inward, so work outside in when you start from a problem.

slides.name: 14 · A threat to validity at each level

params.text: A threat to validity at each level

Domain: you misunderstood their needs.
Abstraction: you’re showing them the wrong thing.
Idiom: the way you show it doesn’t work.
Algorithm: your code is too slow.

slides.notes:
Each level has its own way to fail, and its own way to check: observe users (domain), watch them use it after deployment (abstraction), justify the design against alternatives and test with people (idiom), measure time and memory (algorithm). Work top-down when you start from a problem (problem-driven), bottom-up when you start from a technique.
Source: Munzner (2009); adapted from the supplied Week 3 lecture materials.

slides.name: 18 · Three kinds of attribute

params.text: Pop, Rock, Jazz: labels. You can only tell them apart. Nominal.
S < M < L: an order, but the steps are not measured. Ordinal.
82 is twice 41, and 0 means none. Quantitative.

slides.notes:
2 min, before the recap. Reveal one card at a time and ask what each lets you do: tell values apart, put them in order, measure the gaps. Then the table recaps the three types with more examples.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 3 lecture materials.

slides.name: 19 · Attribute types: the recap

params.data:
Type	What you can do with it	Everyday examples
Nominal (categorical)	Tell values apart: same or different	Fruit, genre, a shirt’s colour
Ordinal	Put values in order: before or after	T-shirt size S, M, L; a star rating; month in a sequence
Quantitative	Measure the gaps, and with a true zero the ratios	Temperature in °C (gaps); price or plays (ratios)

slides.notes:
3 min. Items are the rows (one fruit, one song); attributes are the columns (price, month, genre). Each attribute has a type, and the type limits what a chart may do with it: nominal gets separate hues or positions, ordinal an ordered position or a light-to-dark ramp, quantitative length or position on a scale. Last week’s check used interval and ratio: both are quantitative. Ordered attributes also have a direction (sequential, diverging or cyclic), which comes back with colour scales.
Source: Munzner (2014), Chapter 2.

slides.name: 20 · Check · Semantics decides the type · 1

params.text: A postcode, such as E1 6AN. What type of attribute is it?

slides.notes:
3 min, four quick questions. The point: a number in the file does not make an attribute quantitative. Postcode and shirt number are labels; the star rating is ordered but its gaps are not equal; month is ordered and cyclic. Ask: when would month be quantitative? (Months since launch: elapsed time.)

It contains a number, but E2 is not “more” than E1 and you cannot subtract postcodes. It names a place: nominal.

slides.name: 28 · Keys and values

params.text:
Keys: Fruit + Month identify the observation.
Value: Quantity records how many were sold.

slides.notes:
2 min. Ask: how many apples were sold in April? Point to Apple, then April, then 82. The + means combine two keys, not add their values. In the wide table, Fruit identifies a row and Month identifies a column; together they locate one quantity. In the long table, Fruit + Month identify the observation. Fruit × Month → Quantity is a multidimensional table: one indexed by several keys. Keys are usually categorical or ordinal; values can be of any type. Next ask where Month lives in the supplied table. Reshaping will turn the key hidden in the headings into a column.
Source: Munzner (2014), Chapter 2 (keys and values; multidimensional tables).

slides.notes:
CENTREPIECE: give it time, with discussion before and after. Predict first: most will say Month is “the columns”. That is the point. The table has no Month column; it is wide. Step through:
As supplied: six fruit, three months.
Items: each row is one fruit.
One attribute: April, May and June all hold quantity sold.
Wide to long: every number travels and takes its month with it. 18 rows. This is pandas melt, and Altair’s transform_fold: exactly what Lab 3 needs.
Name the types: Fruit nominal, Month ordinal, Quantity quantitative (ratio: zero means none).

slides.name: 30 · Check · Reshape first · 1

params.text: Country | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 holds GDP. To plot GDP by year, what changes first?
Use each year as a separate line

slides.notes:
2 min. Apply the same move to a new table. Give students 20 seconds to choose, then ask a neighbour why. Collect answers before revealing. Year is hiding in the headings, just as Month was. Reshape to Country | Year | GDP: Country + Year identify a GDP value, Year goes on x and GDP on y. In pandas this is melt; in Altair, transform_fold. If answers split, replay the wide-to-long state. Finish by asking: what stays unchanged? Every GDP value and the country/year it belongs to.

Year becomes a column. Country + Year identify each GDP value. Plot Year on x, GDP on y, and one line per country.

slides.name: 32 · Derived attributes

params.source: Illustrative values, not official trade statistics.
params.prompt: Exports and imports are both measured. Where is the trade balance?

slides.notes:
Derive new attributes from existing ones by arithmetic, logic or statistics. The original slide’s example is trade balance = exports − imports. Step through:
Two measured attributes.
Show the gap: the balance is the distance between the lines, which is hard to judge.
Drop to zero: each gap falls to the baseline keeping its length. Balances: +8, −12, +3, +20, −11, +22.
Running total: cumulative data is derived too: 8, −4, −1, 19, 8, 30.
The Total column in the fruit table was a derived attribute of the same kind.
Step captions in full: Two attributes: Exports and imports over six years, in the same units. Show the gap: The balance is the gap between the lines: blue where exports are higher, orange where imports are. Judging distances between two lines is hard. Drop to zero: Each gap falls to a zero baseline and keeps its length. Trade balance = exports − imports: a new attribute, derived by arithmetic. It can be negative, so zero sits in the middle. Running total: Cumulative data is derived too: add each year’s balance to the years before. Same data, a different question: where do we stand overall?

slides.name: 33 · Section · Why is the user looking?
slides.notes: ≈15 min. The same data answers different questions, and each question wants a different chart.

slides.name: 34 · Search: what do you know already?

params.text: Search: what do you know already?

params.data:
Target known	Target unknown
Location known	Lookup	Browse
Location unknown	Locate	Explore

slides.notes:
Munzner’s four search actions. Lookup: “how many oranges in May?” (you know what and where). Locate: “where is the smallest June value?” Browse: scan one month for anything unusual. Explore: nothing known; look for patterns. The original whiteboard words were Discover, Locate and Compare, and the next slide uses them.
Source: Munzner (2014), Chapter 3.

slides.name: 35 · One table, five questions

params.data:
Fruit	April	May	June
Apple	82	70	20
Pear	73	50	33
Peach	67	45	28
Orange	85	65	17
Kiwi	54	42	24
Melon	33	58	20
params.source: Fruit sales from the NCSS 3D bar chart examples.
params.prompt: Same fruit data. Which chart answers each question fastest?

slides.notes:
Answer key, checked against the table:
Month totals (which month sold most?): April 394, May 330, June 142.
Oranges in May: 65.
Apple v Orange: Apple 82, 70, 20; Orange 85, 65, 17.
The odd one out: Melon, the only fruit up in May (33 → 58).
Fruit totals (which fruit sold most?): Apple 172, then Orange 167.
Also from the original: smallest in June is Orange, 17. After each state ask for the {action, target} pair: discover + extremes, lookup + value, compare + trends, discover + outliers, discover + extremes.
Step captions in full: Month totals: Discover. Summarise over all fruit by adding up each month. April sold most: 394, against 330 in May and 142 in June. These totals are derived; the table never listed them. Oranges in May: Locate one value: 65. Every bar is drawn but only one matters, so the rest step back. For one number, the table would do just as well. Apple v Orange: Compare. Apple 82 → 70 → 20; Orange 85 → 65 → 17. Both fall; Orange starts higher and ends lower. A line suits an ordered attribute like month. The odd one out: Find the anomaly. Five fruit fall from April to May. Melon rises, 33 → 58: the only one. Fruit totals: The months stack into one bar per fruit and sort. Apple leads with 172, just ahead of Orange with 167. Sorting turns find-the-maximum into read-the-first.

slides.name: 39 · Cluster, drawn

params.data:
Song	love	party	heart	dance	baby	night
Song 1	1	8	0	9	2	7
Song 2	8	1	9	0	7	2
Song 3	0	9	1	8	1	8
Song 4	9	2	7	1	8	1
Song 5	2	7	1	9	0	9
Song 6	7	0	8	2	9	1
Song 7	1	8	2	7	1	9
Song 8	8	1	8	1	6	3
params.source: Invented counts for eight songs, built with two groups to find.
params.prompt: Eight songs, six words, how often each is sung. Are there groups of songs?

slides.notes:
The Cluster task as a picture, and the idea behind a clustered heatmap. As collected: noise. Reorder the rows: every cell keeps its value, only the order changes. Reorder the columns: two blocks, ballads (love, heart, baby) and club songs (party, dance, night). A real clustered heatmap finds this order by computing similarity and draws the tree (dendrogram) that joined the rows; the original slide showed one from GeeksforGeeks. Tie it to the How? figure: Arrange → Order. The same move sorted the fruit totals.
Step captions in full: As collected: Darker means the word is sung more. In the order the songs were collected, it looks like noise. Reorder the rows: Only the order of the songs changes. Every cell keeps its value, and a pattern starts to show. Reorder the columns: Put similar words together too and two blocks appear: love, heart, baby songs and party, dance, night songs. That is the Cluster task, and ordering is the channel that reveals it.

slides.name: 40 · Section · How is it shown?

params.text: Data visualisation literacy: critique the chart, not the chart type

slides.name: 41 · From abstraction to idiom

params.text:
Expressiveness: show all of the data’s structure, and only that. Ordered data needs an ordered channel; categories need one that is not ordered.

params.states: [{"label":"Estimate","kind":"channels","focus":0,"labels":false,"explanation":"Estimate each pair before the reveal: B is what % of A?"},{"label":"Position","kind":"channels","focus":0,"labels":true,"explanation":"Position on a common scale: B is 45% of A."},{"label":"Length","kind":"channels","focus":1,"labels":true,"explanation":"Length without a shared baseline: 65%."},{"label":"Angle","kind":"channels","focus":2,"labels":true,"explanation":"Angle, the pie’s channel: 35%, read less accurately."},{"label":"Area","kind":"channels","focus":3,"labels":true,"explanation":"Area: 60%, and usually underestimated."},{"label":"Lightness","kind":"channels","focus":4,"labels":true,"explanation":"Lightness: 50%. Good for order, poor for amount."},{"label":"The ranking","kind":"channels","mode":"ranking","explanation":"Give the most important attribute the most accurate channel."}]
params.source: Constructed mark pairs for estimation. Ranking after Cleveland & McGill (1984) and Heer & Bostock (2010).
params.prompt: Each pair asks the same question: B is what percentage of A? How sure are you of each answer?

slides.notes:
CENTREPIECE: give it time, with discussion before and after. Replay each pair with its true ratio, and compare with the spread of the room’s answers on the previous slide.
Position 45%, Length 65%, Angle 35%, Area 60%, Lightness 50%.
The ranking: position on a common scale, length, angle, area, lightness. Cleveland & McGill measured it in 1984; Heer & Bostock replicated it with crowdsourced participants in 2010. It explains the pie slide coming up (angle and area) and why the rescued 3D chart ended on bars (aligned position).
Source: Cleveland, W. S. & McGill, R. (1984) Graphical Perception, JASA 79(387); Heer, J. & Bostock, M. (2010) Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception, CHI.
Step captions in full: Position: Two dots against one common scale. B is 45% of A. Answers usually cluster tightly here: position on a common scale is the most accurately read channel. Length: Two bars that do not share a baseline, so only their lengths can be compared. B is 65% of A. Without the common baseline, estimates spread wider. Angle: Two wedges from the same starting line. B is 35% of A. Angles are read less accurately than lengths: this is the pie chart’s channel. Area: Two circles. B has 60% of A’s area. Area tends to be underestimated, because the eye compares widths as well as areas. Lightness: Two shades. B is 50% of A. Lightness shows order well (darker is more) but is poor for reading how much more. The ranking: Position on a common scale, length, angle, area, lightness: the order Cleveland and McGill measured in 1984 and Heer and Bostock replicated in 2010. Munzner calls this effectiveness: give the most important attribute the most accurate channel.

slides.name: 55 · Rescue the 3D chart

params.data:
Fruit	April	May	June
Apple	82	70	20
Pear	73	50	33
Peach	67	45	28
Orange	85	65	17

params.prompt: Same fruit, same numbers. What stops you reading this chart, and what would you fix first?

slides.notes:
Take one fix from the room before each state.
3D default: occlusion, perspective, rainbow, walls.
Flatten, stack: depth gone; colour now means month (ordered, so light to dark), but only April shares the baseline.
Side by side: every month starts at zero. Melon stands out.
One question: stack into the derived total and sort. Apple 172.
The fix depends on the task: that is the whole lecture in one slide.
Step captions in full: 3D default: Perspective hides the back rows and makes heights hard to judge. Colour repeats the fruit names already on the axis. The shaded walls add ink but no data. Flatten, stack: Depth gone: nothing is hidden. Colour now shows month, light to dark because months are ordered. But only April sits on the baseline, so comparing May across fruit is hard. Side by side: Every month now starts at zero, so comparing May with May is a length comparison. Melon is the only fruit that sold more in May than in April. One question: If the question is which fruit sells most, stack the months into a derived total and sort. Apple, 172.

slides.name: 58 · Colour follows the ordering

params.data:
Genre	Jan	Feb	Mar	Apr	May	Jun	Jul	Aug	Sep	Oct	Nov	Dec
Pop	3	4	2	-1	-4	-6	-7	-5	-2	1	4	6
Hip-hop	-2	-1	1	3	5	7	8	6	3	0	-2	-3
Rock	1	0	-1	-2	-2	-3	-2	-1	0	1	1	2
Jazz	-4	-3	-2	0	1	2	1	0	-1	-3	-4	-5
Classical	6	5	3	1	-1	-3	-4	-3	-1	2	4	7
params.source: Illustrative values. Colour vision deficiency simulated with Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes (2009), deuteranopia at full severity.
params.prompt: Change in streams against last year, by genre and month. Which cells went up, which went down, and which barely moved?

slides.notes:
CENTREPIECE: give it time, with discussion before and after. 4 min. The ordering direction of an attribute chooses its colour scale.
Sequential: fine for counts, wrong for a signed change, because zero has no colour.
Diverging red–green: right shape, zero palest.
Deuteranopia: the same scale as roughly 1 in 12 men see it. Rises and falls merge.
Blue–orange: diverging, and it survives the simulation.
Cyclic: month wraps round, so December should sit next to January.
Tie back to Access in the five practices: colour with a second cue. Here the second cue is the printed value in each cell.
Source: Munzner (2014), Chapter 10; Machado et al. (2009), IEEE TVCG 15(6).
Step captions in full: Sequential: Light to dark, lowest to highest. But this attribute is signed: the palest cells are the biggest falls, not “no change”, and zero has no colour of its own. Diverging: A diverging scale: zero is palest, falls go one way and rises the other. The attribute’s ordering direction (it diverges from zero) chooses the scale. Deuteranopia: The same red–green scale with deuteranopia simulated (Machado et al., 2009). Around 1 in 12 men have a red–green colour vision deficiency. Rises and falls now look alike. Blue–orange: Still diverging, zero still palest, but blue against orange. Deuteranopia again: Simulated deuteranopia again: rises and falls stay distinct, because blue and orange differ along the blue–yellow axis that deuteranopia keeps. Cyclic months: Month is ordered too, but cyclic: December sits next to January. A sequential scale puts them at opposite ends; a cyclic scale, equally light all the way round the hue wheel, brings them back together.

params.data:
Genre	Share
Pop	40
Hip-hop	25
Rock	20
Jazz	15
params.prompt: Four genres’ share of a playlist. In which version can you tell Hip-hop from Rock most confidently?

slides.notes:
Cleveland and McGill again, from Week 2: aligned position and length beat angle, which beats area. Each state keeps the same four numbers. Ask for a confidence vote before revealing the bars.
Step captions in full: Pie: Angle and area carry the share. Hip-hop (25) and Rock (20) look close. Doughnut: The centre is cut out, so the angle at the middle is gone. You read arc length instead: harder, not easier. Exploded: Pulling the slices apart adds emphasis and separation, but no accuracy. Polar area: Equal angles; the radius changes so that each wedge’s area is its share, as in Nightingale’s rose diagram. Areas are hard to compare. Bars: Aligned length from a common baseline: the most accurate of the five. Hip-hop 25 beats Rock 20 at a glance.

slides.name: 66 · Tables are one of four dataset types

params.text: Tables are one of four dataset types

Tables: items × attributes. The fruit sales, the lyric counts.
Networks: nodes and the links between them. Words sung in the same songs.
Fields: a value at every point in space. Air pollution across London.
Geometry: shapes with a position. Borough boundaries on a map.

Song 1	1	8	0	9	2	7
Song 2	8	1	9	0	7	2
Song 3	0	9	1	8	1	8

params.prompt: The same lyric counts as the heatmap. Could they be a network rather than a table?

slides.notes:
3 min. A table: songs are items, words attributes. Derive pairs: co-occurrence is a derived attribute; the songs disappear and words become the items. A network: nodes are words, links co-occurrence, width how much. Communities: the Cluster task again, found from the links. For the project, a co-occurrence network is a valid abstraction if the question is which words go together; the table is better for how often.
Keep real lyrics off shared slides: use counts, invented lines, or songs out of copyright.
Step captions in full: A table: As collected: a table. The eight songs are the items, the six words are the attributes, and each cell counts how often a word is sung. Derive pairs: A derived table: for each pair of words, add up how often they are sung in the same song (the smaller count, song by song). The songs have gone; words are now the items on both sides. A network: Words become nodes and co-occurrence becomes links. Same data, now abstracted as a network, so network idioms and tasks, such as following paths or finding hubs, become available. Communities: The links split the words into two communities: love, heart, baby and party, dance, night. It is the Cluster task again, found this time from the links rather than by reordering a heatmap.

slides.name: 74 · Takeaways

params.text:
Name the items, the attributes and each attribute’s type. Semantics decides the type, not the file.
Find the keys. If one hides in the headings, reshape wide to long.
Write the task as an {action, target} pair, and derive the attributes it needs.
Choose channels by expressiveness and effectiveness: position first, colour scales that follow the ordering.
Critique a chart against its task, not its type.

slides.notes: 2 min. Ask two students which takeaway they would put first for their project. Then Lab 3: the same moves in Altair.

slides.name: 75 · Reading and sources

params.text:
Munzner (2014): Visualization Analysis and Design, ch. 2, 3 and 5.
Munzner (2009): A Nested Model for Visualization Design.
Amar, Stasko & Eagan (2005): Low-Level Components of Analytic Activity.
Cleveland & McGill (1984); Heer & Bostock (2010): graphical perception.

slides.name: 76 · Q & A

params.text: Ask now, or bring it to the lab.

This night view shows Westminster Bridge and the Palace of Westminster beside the Thames.

Bright lights stand out against the dark sky and water.

The same contrast principle helps important marks stand out in a chart.

slides.notes: Allow 5 min. Likely questions: is month ordinal or quantitative (it depends on the task: as a sequence, ordinal; as elapsed time, interval), and when to melt a table (whenever an attribute is hiding in the headings).

slides.name: 77 · Next: Lab 3 · Data abstraction

params.text:
Pick a Vega dataset and abstract it before you code: goal, domain, abstraction, idiom, algorithm.
Use the pipeline: raw data → table → attributes and types → tasks → visualisation → insight.
Build four charts in Altair: a scatter plot, a line, a bar chart and a stacked bar chart.
Worksheet on Canvas by 12:00 on the Friday after the lab.

slides.notes: The original closing slide said “Next Lesson: Lab 1”; this week’s lab is 03_Lab_IPDV_DataAbstraction. Remind them the reshaping move is what the stacked bar task (iowa_electricity) needs.
